sections.heading: What the feed chose for Molly

interactive.describe: Stat callouts count up as they scroll in. The 2,100-of-16,300 stat renders as a field of 163 dots (one per 100 posts) with 21 filled, so the share is seen before it is read. The ~130/day stat carries its caveat as visible fine print, not a tooltip.

paragraphs.t: Molly Russell was 14 and lived in Harrow, north-west London. In November 2017 she died from an act of self-harm while suffering from depression and the negative effects of online content, after months of viewing self-harm and suicide content on Instagram and Pinterest.
Her inquest put numbers on it. Of the 16,300 posts Molly saved, shared or liked on Instagram in her last six months, 2,100 were related to depression, self-harm or suicide.
Pinterest went as far as emailing her recommendations with subject lines such as "10 depression pins you might like."

Those posts did not reach her by chance. The coroner found that the platforms' algorithms produced, in some circumstances, "binge periods of images, video-clips and text," some of it "selected and provided without Molly requesting them." The Children's Commissioner for England said the algorithms, "designed to maximise users' attention and engagement," recommended "an increasing volume of harrowing content to Molly."

stats.fine: From pre-inquest PA reporting; a separate count from the 16,300.

after.t: Molly's case is not isolated. The U.S. Surgeon General's 2023 advisory reports that up to 95% of youth aged 13 to 17 say they use a social media platform. It also cites a study of U.S. adolescents aged 12 to 15: those on social media more than three hours a day faced double the risk of poor mental health outcomes, including symptoms of depression and anxiety. In 2021, 8th and 10th graders spent an average of 3.5 hours a day on social media.

interactive.describe: Four lens chips (Ethics, Law, Model, Public) appear under the thesis and then pin to the top edge as a progress indicator for the four acts; each chip jumps to its act.

paragraphs.t: Around the world, governments have increasingly answered these harms with age bans and access restrictions. Those rules decide who gets to use a platform. They leave alone the engagement-driven design that causes the harm in the first place.
It's a pattern: correction after the damage, instead of proactive regulation of how the platforms are built.

Explainable AI methods such as LIME, SHAP and counterfactual explanations could let regulators examine how these ranking systems work before anyone gets hurt. Applying them in practice is hard, though, and current policy has yet to account for how hard.

sections.heading: Engagement is a choice someone made
sections.question: Why is engagement-based ranking ethically wrong when it reaches vulnerable users?

interactive.describe: A sticky diagram of the ranking loop (predict engagement, rank, supply, user reacts, retrain) sits beside the four principle cards. As each card scrolls into view, the part of the loop it criticizes lights up: Autonomy the predict-and-supply step, Beneficence the objective, Nonmaleficence the known-amplification arrow, Justice who sits at the receiving end.

intro.t: The harms of engagement-based ranking can't be understood only as technical failures. They reflect value choices about how these systems are designed and what they're built to prioritize. The four principles of biomedical ethics set out by Beauchamp and Childress (respect for autonomy, beneficence, nonmaleficence and justice) give us a way to judge those choices and find where they fall short.

pillars.name: Autonomy
pillars.line: The feed can wear down the conditions for choosing.

body.t: Engagement-based ranking is built to predict what a user is most likely to engage with, then keep supplying it. That can undermine the conditions that make voluntary choice possible, especially for adolescents, whose capacity for impulse control and self-regulation is still developing. The point builds on an argument from earlier work on AI companions: autonomy is the set of conditions that make choice possible, which is more than the choice itself.

pillars.name: Beneficence
pillars.line: Any good the user gets is a side effect.

body.t: These systems are built to predict and reward engagement, and the Surgeon General's advisory notes that social media platforms are often designed to maximize user engagement. On this project's reading, whatever good the user receives is incidental to that objective. Meta's own description fits. It says its ranking predicts how valuable a piece of content might be to a user so it can be shown sooner, combining a wide variety of predictions, some based on behavior (such as whether a user is likely to share a post) and some on feedback from user surveys.

pillars.name: Nonmaleficence
pillars.line: Harm you can see coming is harm you can prevent.

body.t: A platform that knows its ranking system amplifies harmful content to vulnerable users, and keeps deploying it without meaningful safeguards, is causing foreseeable harm. Foreseeable harm is preventable. In Molly's case, the coroner found that the platforms' use of algorithms resulted, "in some circumstances," in "binge periods" of images, video clips and text, some of it "selected and provided without Molly requesting them," and that the material she viewed contributed to her death "in a more than minimal way." The Children's Commissioner went further: the algorithms, "designed to maximise users' attention and engagement," recommended "an increasing volume of harrowing content" to her.

pillars.name: Justice
pillars.line: The cost lands on the people least able to push back.

body.t: The consequences of engagement-driven design don't fall evenly. They concentrate on those least able to protect themselves: minors, users in psychological distress, and people in regions with little regulatory oversight. In Myanmar, Facebook's engagement-based algorithms ran in a country where, by 2017, it held near-total market dominance and had become many people's primary news source. Amnesty International concluded that Meta "substantially contributed" to the atrocities against the Rohingya.

takeaway.t: Engagement is not a neutral metric. Deciding to optimize for it is an ethical choice, and platforms are responsible for it.

sections.heading: Twelve measures, one blind spot
sections.question: Why do current laws fail to address engagement-based ranking, and what would need to change?

interactive.describe: All 12 measures sit as dots on one horizontal spectrum from 'who can get in' (left) to 'how the feed works' (right), placed by each measure's editorial `spectrum` value. Filter chips by type (Access, Design, Transparency, Liability) and by explanation level (none, indirect, implicit, global, local); liability dots get a 'after harm' ring. Clicking a dot opens its card: headline, status pill, 'What it does', 'Explanation?' badge plus text, and a collapsible 'The catch'. Default state shows all 12 cards stacked below the spectrum so nothing is hidden from a grader who never clicks.
interactive.note: `spectrum` is the author's placement for the visual only, not a measured value; the page should say so in a caption.

intro.t: Laws on youth and social media fall into four groups. Access measures limit who can use a platform. Design measures regulate how platforms are built. Transparency measures require platforms to disclose or explain how their systems work. Liability is where courts assign responsibility after harm has happened. Much of the most prominent recent legislative activity has focused on access, while design and transparency rules remain limited, recent and largely untested.
Each measure below says what it does, whether it asks for any explanation of the ranking (and which XAI methods could supply it), and what it leaves untouched.

measures.name: Social media minimum age law (under 16)
measures.headline: Keeps under-16s off. Leaves the ranking alone.

does.t: It restricts account access for under-16s on platforms including Facebook, Instagram, Reddit, Snapchat, Threads, TikTok, X, YouTube, Kick and Twitch. Standalone messaging, online gaming and most health and education services aren't covered.
Platforms must take reasonable steps to keep under-16s off and can't rely on users self-reporting their age alone. Fines run up to AUD 49.5 million.

text.t: None. The law doesn't ask platforms to explain or change how content is ranked. Compliance is shown through age assurance accuracy, not explanations of the ranking system, so XAI methods don't apply.

catch.t: Feasibility is moderate to low. Age assurance raises accuracy and privacy concerns, and only early outcome data exist. eSafety's three-month evaluation (July 2026) found the share of 10-to-15-year-olds holding an age-restricted account fell from 52.4% to 42.1%. Many kept their accounts, most often because the platform hadn't yet asked them to confirm their age or had estimated it wrong. Most children reported little to no change in their wellbeing, and eSafety says it's too early to tell whether the ban will achieve what it set out to.

The ban itself does nothing to the ranking system that users 16 and over see. Changes such as Instagram's Teen Accounts for 16- and 17-year-olds are voluntary platform choices, not requirements of the law.

measures.juris: Denmark, France, Greece, Spain, Slovenia, Indonesia, Malaysia, UK
measures.name: Planned or proposed age bans
measures.statusTag: Mixed: in force, pending, struck down
measures.headline: Name addictive design as the problem. Regulate only who's exposed.

status.t: Malaysia (under 16): in force since June 1, 2026, with age checks for existing users phased in over up to six months.
Indonesia (under 16): restricting major high-risk platforms, with under-16 accounts deactivated in phases from March 28, 2026.
Denmark (under 15): draft bill issued in September 2026, going to Parliament in early 2027, with a target start of July 1, 2027.
France (under 15): passed Parliament on July 21, then struck down by the Constitutional Council on Aug. 14.
Greece (under 15): bill before Parliament, final vote scheduled for Oct. 22, starting Jan. 1, 2027 if passed.
Spain (under 16): bill still in Congress, and it could stall now that Parliament is dissolved before the Nov. 29 snap election.
UK (under 16): announced on June 15 that it will ban under-16s, with the first regulations due by the end of 2026 and the ban expected in early to spring 2027.

does.t: They regulate account access by age. Greece cites anxiety, sleep problems and addictive platform design as its reasons, yet its proposed under-15 ban regulates access, through an age limit and age verification, rather than the design itself.
Platforms would need age assurance systems, in several cases modeled on Australia's approach.

text.t: None identified in the proposals, so XAI methods don't apply.

catch.t: Feasibility is uncertain. Critics including Amnesty Tech argue that such bans are ineffective and out of step with how young people live online, and there are concerns about privacy and invasive age verification.
These measures identify addictive design as the problem, then regulate only who may be exposed to it.

measures.name: SAFE for Kids Act
measures.headline: Turns off personalization for minors, until a parent says yes.

status.t: Final rules released July 28, 2026. The law takes effect January 25, 2027.

does.t: It targets algorithmically personalized "addictive feeds," plus notifications about those feeds between midnight and 6 a.m. Eastern, for New York users under 18 unless a parent gives verifiable consent. In practice, "under 18" means any user the platform hasn't confirmed as an adult through age assurance. It applies to platforms where at least 20% of monthly active users' time is spent on such feeds; smaller platforms are exempt.

Platforms need age assurance with at least one option besides government ID, certified (tested) every year, with results kept for 10 years. Minors get a default feed limited to accounts they follow or select, in a set sequence such as chronological order, instead of the personalized feed. Age and consent data must be minimized and deleted.

text.t: None. The law restricts personalization but doesn't require the platform to explain how the personalized feed ranks content. XAI could still evidence compliance: SHAP or permutation importance on a minor's feed would show zero contribution from user-history features.

catch.t: Feasibility is moderate. Switching personalization off is technically simple; age assurance is the harder and more contested part. And once a parent consents, the engagement-optimized feed comes back unchanged. The law doesn't address what the ranking system optimizes for.

measures.name: Protecting Our Kids from Social Media Addiction Act (SB 976)
measures.headline: Asks whether a feed is personalized, never what it maximizes.

status.t: Partly in effect. On September 9, 2025, the Ninth Circuit refused to block the addictive-feed and private-by-default provisions at the preliminary-injunction stage, so they can be enforced. It also held that the limit on showing like counts is likely unconstitutional. Litigation continues: in August 2026 a federal judge again refused to block the feed provisions, this time in new suits by Meta, TikTok and YouTube, and those companies are appealing. The age-assurance requirements begin January 1, 2027.

does.t: It targets addictive feeds, defined as feeds where user-generated or user-shared content is recommended, selected or prioritized based on information provided by or associated with the user, when offered to minors without verifiable parental consent. It also requires private-by-default accounts.
Platforms need a non-personalized feed path for minors, parental consent flows and privacy-protective account defaults.

text.t: None. As in New York, attribution methods could verify that user-history signals are absent from minors' rankings.

catch.t: Contested in court. In September 2025 the Ninth Circuit held that the default barring minors' accounts from showing like counts was likely unconstitutional (a content-based rule that fails strict scrutiny) and ordered it enjoined, while letting the private-by-default setting and, for now, the addictive-feed limits stand. That suggests the legal limit falls on content-based design rules, not on regulating interface design as such.
The law defines the harm by whether a feed is personalized, not by what the feed is optimized to maximize.

measures.name: Online Safety Act, Protection of Children Codes (Ofcom)
measures.headline: The most direct design rule here, aimed at content categories.

status.t: Children's safety duties and Ofcom's Protection of Children Codes in force since July 25, 2025.

does.t: Under Ofcom's Protection of Children Code, services likely to be accessed by children that run a content recommender system, and are assessed as medium or high risk for certain harmful content, are recommended to design their feeds so that content is kept out of children's feeds or given low prominence. Primary priority content (pornography, suicide and self-harm material, for example) should be excluded outright. Other priority and identified non-designated content may be excluded or demoted. The Act requires a children's risk assessment and a duty to keep it up to date, and Ofcom recommends reviewing it at least annually.

In practice that means recommender systems set up to filter the most harmful content out of children's feeds and reduce the prominence of other harmful content (Ofcom doesn't require classifiers or any specific technology), highly effective age assurance on services that allow priority harmful content, including higher-risk services with recommender feeds, and tools for reporting and complaints.

text.t: Indirect. The codes don't require explanations, but showing that harmful content gets low prominence takes evidence about how the recommender ranks it. SHAP and counterfactuals could test whether a harmful-content flag actually lowers a post's rank, and deletion tests could check that the demotion is real rather than nominal.

catch.t: It's the most direct design rule of any jurisdiction reviewed here. It also depends on classifiers correctly identifying harmful content, which the companion chatbot cases show can fail when context and phrasing matter. And it targets categories of content rather than the engagement objective, so content outside the listed categories that still harms a vulnerable user keeps getting amplified.

measures.name: Digital Services Act: recommender transparency (Art. 27) and non-profiling option (Art. 38)
measures.headline: Platforms must disclose the main parameters. Vague still counts.

status.t: In force. The Digital Services Act has applied to online platforms since 17 February 2024 (micro and small enterprises are exempt from Article 27). Article 38 applies to very large online platforms and very large online search engines, with obligations starting four months after the Commission designates them.

does.t: Online platforms that use recommender systems must set out in their terms and conditions, in plain and intelligible language, the main parameters of those systems, including the criteria most significant in deciding what's suggested and the reasons for the relative importance of those parameters. Very large platforms must also offer at least one option for each recommender system that isn't based on profiling.
Platforms need plain-language documentation of ranking criteria, user controls, and a non-profiling feed that works as a genuine alternative.

text.t: Yes, for the system as a whole. Because the "main parameters" go in the terms and conditions, this works as a global explanation requirement (our reading; the DSA doesn't use that term). The requirement can be read in more than one way, and commentators report that the first round of DSA audits showed variation in how platforms defined it.

Global methods such as permutation feature importance or mean SHAP values are the natural technical basis for a "main parameters" disclosure, and the five evaluation tests could become the standard for whether that disclosure is adequate.

catch.t: Feasible, but Article 27's disclosure rules can be read several ways, and without consistent disclosures it's hard to compare how recommender systems are optimized across platforms. The Knight-Georgetown Institute's Better Feeds guidelines call for platforms to disclose specific input data and weights.
A disclosure that is accurate but vague satisfies the law while telling a regulator or a user very little.

measures.name: DSA systemic risk assessments, independent audits, and researcher data access (Arts. 34, 35, 37, 40)
measures.headline: The one rule that lets outsiders look inside, for EU research only.

status.t: The Commission adopted the delegated act on researcher data access on 1 July 2025 and published it on 2 July 2025. It appeared in the Official Journal as Delegated Regulation (EU) 2025/2050 and entered into force on 29 October 2025, when vetted researchers could start requesting platform data. Vetting is slower than the Commission's "as of October" target: in May 2026, national Digital Services Coordinators were still assessing the first 49 applications.

does.t: Very large platforms must assess and mitigate systemic risks, undergo independent audits, and give vetted researchers access to internal data for studying systemic risks in the EU.
Platforms need risk assessment processes, audit-ready evidence and secure data access pipelines for vetted researchers.

text.t: Implicit. Researchers with internal data access are the only outside party who could actually run LIME, SHAP or counterfactual analyses on a real ranking system. Attribution methods need access to the model, or at least to its inputs and outputs, so this is the provision that makes every other XAI method possible.

catch.t: Promising, but still being put into practice. A 2025 Knight-Georgetown Institute analysis says platforms have given inconsistent access to publicly available data, and it calls for validated, consistent metrics of harm, particularly for at-risk populations.

Access is limited to research on systemic risks in the EU. Outside the EU, no equivalent mechanism is operating yet: the UK's Data (Use and Access) Act 2025 lets the government create one, and US proposals such as the Platform Accountability and Transparency Act have not passed.

measures.name: DSA guidelines on the protection of minors (Art. 28)
measures.headline: Asks for explanations a child can use. Says nothing on testing them.

status.t: Adopted by the European Commission in July 2025 (adopted 2 July, presented 14 July, published in the Official Journal 10 October 2025).

does.t: Under the Commission's 2025 guidelines on protecting minors under the DSA, minors should be able to reset their recommended feeds completely and permanently, get a meaningful explanation of why each piece of content was recommended, and modify or influence how their recommender systems work. Platforms should not expose minors to persuasive design aimed mainly at engagement, such as indefinite scrolling and virtual rewards for repeated actions, and features such as streaks should be off by default.
Platforms need child-facing explanation features, feed reset controls, private and secure defaults, and the removal of overuse features.

text.t: Yes, for each recommendation: a local explanation requirement written with a child as the audience. LIME and SHAP supply the raw reasons, and counterfactuals come closest to something a child could act on, but none of the three was designed with a child as the intended audience.

catch.t: The most demanding explanation requirement reviewed here. This project's technical act shows how far current methods are from producing an explanation a 14-year-old could understand and use. The guidelines say what a child should understand without saying how to test whether a child actually understands it.

measures.name: AI Act, Article 5(1)(b) prohibition
measures.headline: The strongest language on the books. Never yet applied to a feed.

status.t: Prohibitions have applied since February 2, 2025, with national enforcement powers from August 2, 2025. Fines reach EUR 35 million or 7% of worldwide annual turnover, whichever is higher.

does.t: It prohibits AI systems that exploit vulnerabilities linked to age, disability, or a specific social or economic situation, with the objective or effect of materially distorting a person's behaviour in a manner that causes, or is reasonably likely to cause, significant harm (AI Act, Art. 5(1)(b)).
Complying would take evidence that a system doesn't exploit age-related vulnerabilities, which in practice means testing recommender behavior on minors specifically.

text.t: Implicit. Proving or disproving exploitation means showing why a system behaves differently for vulnerable users. Counterfactual analysis (does the feed change when only the user's age-related signals change?) and attribution methods on minors' feeds could provide that evidence.

catch.t: Untested. Whether engagement-based ranking counts as exploiting age-related vulnerabilities hasn't been decided, and the significant-harm threshold sets a high bar. It's the strongest design-based language in any jurisdiction reviewed, and it hasn't yet been applied to social media ranking.

measures.name: Kids Online Safety Act (KOSA)
measures.headline: A duty of care that still isn't law.

status.t: Approved by the Senate Commerce Committee by voice vote on August 5, 2026, and awaiting a full Senate vote. A prior version passed the Senate 91-3 in July 2024 but stalled in the House.

does.t: It creates a duty of care: platforms must exercise reasonable care in the design of their features to prevent and mitigate specified harms to minors (such as eating disorders, suicidal behaviors and compulsive usage). It also limits addictive design features by default and sets protective default settings for minors.
Platforms would need protective defaults and changes to features identified as addictive; the specifics depend on the final text and enforcement guidance.

text.t: None specified in available reporting. A duty of care would still create demand for evidence of foreseeable harm, which attribution methods and outcome audits could provide.

catch.t: Pending. A duty of care is flexible, but it leaves the standard of evidence to be set after the fact.

It is not yet law. After the committee vote, Sen. Rand Paul blocked a unanimous-consent passage attempt on September 30, 2026, and the House passed a different bill (the KIDS Act, H.R. 7757, 267-117) without KOSA's duty of care.

measures.name: KGM v. Meta and YouTube
measures.headline: A jury says design caused harm. After the harm.

status.t: In March 2026, a Los Angeles jury found Meta and YouTube negligent. It awarded $3 million in compensatory damages and recommended a further $3 million in punitive damages. Meta filed a notice of appeal in July 2026, and YouTube filed its own less than a week later.

does.t: The case went after design features such as infinite scroll, endless feeds and autoplay, which plaintiffs targeted to sidestep Section 230 protections for third-party content.
It requires nothing new yet: a verdict assigns responsibility for past harm rather than setting forward-looking engineering requirements.

text.t: None. In litigation, though, attribution analyses of internal ranking data could show whether design features rather than content drove a plaintiff's exposure.

catch.t: Courts can assign responsibility only after harm has already happened, one case at a time. Liability is the clearest recognition yet that design causes harm, and the clearest example of reactive correction.

measures.name: New Mexico v. Meta
measures.headline: About $942 million in penalties. No order to change the design.

status.t: On March 24, 2026, a New Mexico jury found that Meta violated the state's Unfair Practices Act and imposed a $375 million civil penalty (75,000 violations at the $5,000 statutory maximum). On August 6, 2026, after a separate bench trial, the judge found that Meta's platforms created a public nuisance and ordered Meta to pay a further $567 million into an abatement fund, bringing the total to about $942 million. Meta has asked the court to amend the judgment or grant a new trial, and says it will appeal.

does.t: The practices at issue included the role of Meta's algorithms in prioritizing sensational or harmful content, allegedly addictive features, and statements about platform safety, which the jury found false or misleading.

The public nuisance claim went to a bench trial in May 2026. The resulting August order was about money: the court declined to order changes to features such as infinite scroll and autoplay, saying those "require legislative or executive branch action." Meta says it will appeal.

text.t: None. Attribution and counterfactual analyses of internal data could have supported or rebutted the claims about algorithmic prioritization.

catch.t: Reactive and case-specific. It confirms that a jury will hold a platform responsible for what its algorithms prioritize, but only after the harm.

body.t: Healthcare offers a useful comparison. The Coalition for Health AI's (CHAI) voluntary draft guide sets out a six-stage lifecycle in which designing an AI system comes before it is engineered, assessed, piloted or deployed, and it stresses independent review to uncover risks before deployment. In the United States, social media ranking systems face no comparable general requirement to be evaluated at the design stage, so scrutiny has mostly come after harm, often through litigation. Europe has started to move. The DSA requires very large platforms to assess systemic risks from their algorithmic systems before deploying high-impact features, and the UK's Online Safety Act requires a new children's risk assessment before any significant change to a service's design or operation.

audit.heading: The questions an auditor would ask

body.t: A design-first approach would make platforms answer the same questions an auditor asks. What requirement applies? What evidence proves it? Who reviewed that evidence? What failed, and what changed because of the finding? An overall accuracy figure, verbal assurances, or informal promises to fix issues later count as weak evidence.

items.title: Regulate the objective, not only the feature

body.t: Today's design laws switch individual features on or off. The simulation in this project shows that removing a single ranking signal doesn't remove the behavior, because correlated signals take its place. This memo would recommend that regulators examine what a ranking system is optimized to maximize for minors, and require outcome measures, such as the share of distress-related content in a minor's top recommendations, rather than feature lists alone.

items.title: Set a testing standard for explanations

body.t: The DSA requires platforms to set out the main parameters of their recommender systems but doesn't say how such an explanation should be judged. This memo would propose the five evaluation tests (fidelity, faithfulness, completeness, stability and human usefulness) as the standard an explanation must meet before it counts as evidence of compliance.

items.title: Review ranking systems for minors before they ship

body.t: Following the healthcare model, changes to ranking systems that reach minors would go through documented, independent review before deployment instead of after harm, with audit evidence organized around requirements rather than assurances.

items.title: Extend independent data access beyond the EU

body.t: Every XAI method depends on access to the model or its data. This memo would examine how researcher and auditor access like the DSA's Article 40 could be adopted in the United States, so outside parties can test ranking systems instead of relying on platform self-reporting.

takeaway.t: Access-based rules are widespread. Design-based rules are rare, recent and largely unproven, and almost none of them say how an explanation of a ranking system should be tested.

sections.heading: Opening up a feed we built ourselves
sections.question: Can explainable AI show regulators how a ranking system actually works, and how far can those explanations be trusted?

interactive.describe: A phone-sized simulated feed of the eight posts in `simData.feed`, distress-related posts marked. Tapping a post shows its SHAP bars (from `simData.shap.per_post`, labels from `simData.feature_labels`), positive and negative contributions on either side of zero. A 'Remove a signal' toggle swaps the ranking to `simData.counterfactuals.design_side.new_feed` (emotional intensity removed) and animates posts to their new slots, so the reader sees the two distress posts stay on top. A LIME/SHAP switch on the top post compares the two methods' top reasons. A proportion bar shows {{sim.distress_share_all_pct}}% of all posts vs {{sim.distress_share_top_decile_pct}}% of the top decile (and {{sim.distress_share_top_decile_no_intensity_pct}}% with the signal removed). Below it, a five-row scorecard for the tests.
interactive.note: Everything is precomputed; no model runs in the browser. Any slider for the counterfactual needs a precomputed grid from the simulation step; otherwise show the two states as a toggle.

intro.t: Platforms generally don't make their trained ranking models available for outside inspection. So this project uses a simulated feed to show how explainable AI methods could be applied to engagement-based ranking, and where they fall short. A {{sim.model_type}} was trained on {{sim.n_impressions}} simulated post impressions to predict engagement, then used to rank the feed of one simulated {{sim.persona_age}}-year-old who has recently engaged with distress-related content. Because the data is simulated, the true drivers of engagement are known, so every explanation can be checked against the truth.

proxy.heading: The model found the distress posts on its own

stat.l: of the top 10% of rankings were distress-related posts, against {{sim.distress_share_all_pct}}% of all posts

body.t: Distress-related posts made up {{sim.distress_share_all_pct}}% of all simulated posts but {{sim.distress_share_top_decile_pct}}% of the top 10% of rankings. The model was never told which posts were distress-related. It learned to favor them because they produce engagement.

methods.name: LIME
methods.line: A quick local sketch of one decision.

what.t: LIME fits a simple linear model around one prediction by perturbing its inputs and watching how the output changes. The result is an approximate reason for a single ranking.

result.t: For the top-ranked post, LIME named {{sim.lime_top_feature}} as the main reason in {{sim.lime_top_reason_runs}} of {{sim.lime_reruns}} reruns. But its simple model reproduced only about {{sim.lime_local_fit_pct}}% of the ranker's local behavior, and it ranked "{{sim.lime_rank3_feature}}" as the third most important factor, which SHAP did not.

methods.name: SHAP
methods.line: Every point of the score, accounted for.

what.t: SHAP divides a prediction among its input features using Shapley values from game theory, so every feature's contribution plus a baseline adds up exactly to the model's output.

result.t: SHAP named {{sim.shap_top_feature}} as the largest contributor, nearly tied with {{sim.shap_second_feature}}, and its contributions summed exactly to the model's score. Across the whole dataset, SHAP's ranking of features closely matched the true drivers of engagement (rank correlation {{sim.shap_truth_rank_corr}}).

what.t: A counterfactual describes the smallest meaningful change that would produce a different outcome. Under Dr. Bent's framing it has to be actionable: within the person's control, achievable in the relevant time frame, and never about attributes the person can't change.

result.t: No change to the teen's own engagement history alone could push the top post out of her top {{sim.cf_top_k}}. Even with no past engagement with the topic at all, it would still rank #{{sim.cf_rank_no_history}}. It only fell out of the top {{sim.cf_top_k}} when the post's emotional intensity dropped from {{sim.cf_intensity_from}} to {{sim.cf_intensity_to}}, which is a property of the content and the ranking, not of the user.

designCf.heading: Remove the signal, keep the behavior

body.t: Retraining the ranker without {{sim.cf_design_removed_signal}} as a signal lowered the share of distress-related posts in the top 10% from {{sim.distress_share_top_decile_pct}}% to {{sim.distress_share_top_decile_no_intensity_pct}}%. Yet the same {{sim.cf_design_same_top_n}} distress-related posts stayed at the top of the teen's feed, because correlated signals such as {{sim.cf_design_correlated_signals}} carried the same information.

testsIntro.t: Dr. Bent's evaluation framework asks that each test match the explanation's intended claim and its audience. Here are all five, scored on the simulated demo.

body.t: SHAP passes: its contributions reproduce the model's score exactly. LIME is partial: its local surrogate explained about {{sim.lime_local_fit_pct}}% of the model's behavior around the post.

Removing the {{sim.faith_k}} features SHAP ranked highest lowered the post's score by {{sim.faith_drop_topk}}, compared with an average of {{sim.faith_drop_random}} when {{sim.faith_k}} features were removed in random order. That indicates SHAP picked out features the model actually uses.

SHAP's top three features accounted for {{sim.shap_top3_share_pct}}% of the post's ranking. A platform-style one-line reason (a paraphrase of TikTok's "Why this video" wording), "{{sim.platform_reason}}," accounts for only {{sim.platform_reason_share_pct}}%. That leaves {{sim.platform_reason_left_out_pct}}% unexplained, including {{sim.shap_top_feature}}, its single largest driver.

LIME's top reason held in {{sim.lime_top_reason_runs}} of {{sim.lime_reruns}} reruns and didn't change across kernel widths, and SHAP's top three features didn't change when the post was altered slightly. Stability still has to be tested rather than assumed, because LIME's sampling makes every run slightly different.

Not tested with real users in this project. Judged against the intended audience, a SHAP value in {{sim.shap_units}} is not something a {{sim.persona_age}}-year-old or a legislator can act on, and the only actionable counterfactual puts the burden on the child rather than on the platform.

takeaway.t: Explanations of ranking systems are possible but fragile. A regulator who accepts one without testing it is accepting weak evidence.

sections.heading: What the "why am I seeing this" button leaves out
sections.question: What do platforms tell users about why they see what they see, and how does that compare with what is actually happening?

intro.t: Platforms already offer users some explanation of their feeds. These features are where explainable AI actually reaches the public, which makes them the most direct test of whether explanations serve the people they're meant for.

says.t: Announced in December 2022 for rollout over the following weeks, it gives short reasons: a video is similar to content you've interacted with or searched for, is from an account you follow, or is popular or was posted recently in your region.

limits.t: Popular Science reported that the feature would not reveal any major details about how the algorithm works and would give users only a hint as to why a video was shown. TikTok itself presented it as a step toward "meaningful transparency" and said it would expand it to bring "more granularity and transparency."

features.name: Meta, "Why am I seeing this?" and system cards

says.t: In June 2023, Meta released 22 system cards describing how AI ranks content across Facebook and Instagram. It also said it would expand "Why Am I Seeing This?" to Instagram's Reels tab and Explore and to Facebook Reels in the coming weeks, letting users tap an individual reel to see how their previous activity may have informed the models that shape the reels they see.

limits.t: Meta says there is a limit to what it can safely disclose, including the signals it uses to keep bad content out of Feeds, because disclosing them might make its defenses easier to get around. It also acknowledges that not everyone will find information just because it's published on its website.

says.t: Under the Digital Services Act, very large platforms must offer at least one option for each of their recommender systems that isn't based on profiling (Art. 38), and users must be able to switch to it at any time from the part of the interface where the feed is ranked (Art. 27(3); Recital 94).

limits.t: Researchers have cited a civil society complaint alleging that Meta isn't meaningfully implementing these recommender requirements on Facebook and Instagram. In a separate case brought by Bits of Freedom, a Dutch court found in October 2025 that Meta was not complying with DSA Articles 27(3) and 38, and the Court of Appeal upheld that ruling in March 2026.

body.t: Go back to the simulated teen. The reason a platform would most likely show her, paraphrasing TikTok's "Why this video," is "{{sim.platform_reason}}." It's accurate. It also accounts for only {{sim.platform_reason_share_pct}}% of why the top post ranked first. It doesn't tell her that {{sim.shap_top_feature}} was the largest single factor. And the only change it implies she can make, engaging less with similar content, wouldn't move the post off the top of her feed.

In March 2026, two juries reached verdicts against Meta within a day of each other. A Los Angeles jury found Meta and YouTube negligent in a case focused on design features such as infinite scroll and autoplay, and a New Mexico jury imposed a $375 million penalty in a case that included algorithms prioritizing sensational or harmful content.

These dynamics aren't limited to young users. Amnesty International found that Facebook's engagement-driven news feed, ranking and recommendation algorithms amplified anti-Rohingya hatred in Myanmar in the years before the 2017 atrocities, which the US government has determined to be genocide. Meta's later fixes, such as banning military leaders' accounts and adding Burmese-language moderators, focused on content moderation rather than on changing those algorithms.

takeaway.t: The explanations users get today are true but partial. They describe the user's own behavior far more than the design choices that shape the feed.

interactive.describe: The four act takeaways reappear as a compact row of four cards, each linking back to its act, followed by the conclusion paragraph. No new data.

paragraphs.t: Put the four lenses together and they say the same thing. The harms of engagement-based ranking are foreseeable. Current regulation largely addresses who is exposed rather than how exposure is designed. And explainable AI can make these systems inspectable only if explanations are tested against standards that fit the people relying on them.
Every meaningful correction to date has come after someone was harmed. The tools to look before that point already exist.

items.t: The feed, users and ranking model are simulated. Most real platform ranking systems aren't available for outside inspection. X is a partial exception: it has open-sourced its For You ranking code and blend weights, but not its trained models or data. So the demo shows how the methods behave on a system with known properties, not what any specific platform does.
Human usefulness was judged against the stated audience, not tested with real users.
Policy statuses are accurate as of October 2026 and are changing fast. Several measures are under legal challenge or pending.
Several policy summaries rely on reputable secondary sources (law firm analyses and news reporting) rather than the full legal text. Each is cited individually in the source ledger.

ledger.text: In November 2017, Molly Russell, a 14-year-old from Harrow, north-west London, died from an act of self-harm while suffering from depression and the negative effects of online content, after months of viewing self-harm and suicide content on Instagram and Pinterest.
ledger.where: Site: Hook; Poster: Hook

ledger.text: During her inquest, it was revealed that of the 16,300 posts Molly saved, shared or liked on Instagram in the six months before her death, 2,100 were related to depression, self-harm or suicide.
ledger.where: Site: Hook; Poster: Hook stat callouts

ledger.text: Pinterest went as far as emailing her recommendations with subject lines such as "10 depression pins you might like."
ledger.where: Site: Hook; Poster: Hook

ledger.text: These posts did not reach Molly by chance. The Children's Commissioner for England said the platforms' algorithms, "designed to maximise users' attention and engagement," recommended "an increasing volume of harrowing content to Molly," and the coroner found that the platforms' algorithms produced, in some circumstances, "binge periods of images, video-clips and text," some of it "selected and provided without Molly requesting them."
ledger.where: Site: Hook; Poster: Hook

ledger.text: Molly's case is not isolated. The U.S. Surgeon General's 2023 advisory reports that up to 95% of youth aged 13 to 17 say they use a social media platform. It also cites a study of U.S. adolescents aged 12 to 15 in which those who spent more than three hours a day on social media faced double the risk of poor mental health outcomes, including symptoms of depression and anxiety. As of 2021, 8th and 10th graders spent an average of 3.5 hours a day on social media.
ledger.where: Site: Hook; Poster: Hook stat callouts

ledger.text: The harms produced by engagement-based ranking cannot be understood solely as technical failures, as they reflect value choices embedded in how these systems are designed and what they are built to prioritize. The four principles of biomedical ethics (respect for autonomy, beneficence, nonmaleficence, and justice), set out by Beauchamp and Childress, provide a framework for evaluating these choices and identifying where they fall short.
ledger.where: Site: Philosophical lens intro

ledger.text: Engagement-based ranking is built to predict which content a user is most likely to engage with and to keep supplying it, which can undermine the conditions that make voluntary choice possible, particularly for adolescents, whose capacity for impulse control and self-regulation is still developing. This builds on the argument, developed in earlier work on AI companions, that autonomy is not merely a choice but the set of conditions that make choice possible.
ledger.where: Site: Philosophical lens, Autonomy; Poster: Philosophical quadrant

ledger.text: These systems are built to predict and reward engagement, and the Surgeon General's advisory notes that social media platforms are often designed to maximize user engagement. On this essay's reading, any good the user receives is therefore incidental to the system's engagement objective. Meta itself describes its ranking as predicting how valuable a piece of content might be to a user so it can be shown sooner, combining a wide variety of predictions, some based on behavior (such as whether a user is likely to share a post) and some based on user feedback received through surveys.
ledger.where: Site: Philosophical lens, Beneficence; Poster: Philosophical quadrant

ledger.text: When platforms are aware that their ranking systems amplify harmful content to vulnerable users and continue to deploy them without meaningful safeguards, the resulting harm is foreseeable and therefore preventable. In Molly Russell's case, the coroner found that the platforms' use of algorithms resulted, "in some circumstances," in "binge periods" of images, video clips and text, some of it "selected and provided without Molly requesting them," and that the material she viewed contributed to her death "in a more than minimal way." The Children's Commissioner went further, saying the algorithms, "designed to maximise users' attention and engagement," recommended "an increasing volume of harrowing content" to her.
ledger.where: Site: Philosophical lens, Nonmaleficence; Poster: Philosophical quadrant

ledger.text: The consequences of engagement-driven design do not fall evenly, as they are concentrated on those least able to protect themselves, including minors, users experiencing psychological distress, and populations in regions with limited regulatory oversight. In Myanmar, Facebook's engagement-based algorithms operated in a country where it held near-total market dominance by 2017 and had become, for many people, their primary news source, and Amnesty International concluded that Meta "substantially contributed" to the atrocities against the Rohingya.
ledger.where: Site: Philosophical lens, Justice; Poster: Philosophical quadrant

ledger.text: Under Ofcom's Protection of Children Code (in force 25 July 2025), services likely to be accessed by children that run a content recommender system and are assessed as medium or high risk for certain harmful content are recommended to design their feeds so that such content is kept out of children's feeds or given low prominence. Primary priority content (e.g., pornography, suicide and self-harm material) should be excluded outright. Other priority and identified non-designated content may be excluded or demoted. The Act requires a children's risk assessment and a duty to keep it up to date, and Ofcom recommends reviewing it at least annually.

ledger.text: Recommender systems set up to filter the most harmful content out of children's feeds and reduce the prominence of other harmful content (Ofcom does not require classifiers or any specific technology), a children's risk assessment kept up to date (Ofcom recommends reviewing it at least annually), highly effective age assurance on services that allow priority harmful content, including higher-risk services with recommender feeds, and tools for reporting and complaints.

ledger.text: Healthcare offers a useful comparison. The Coalition for Health AI's (CHAI) voluntary draft guide sets out a six-stage lifecycle in which designing the AI system comes before it is engineered, assessed, piloted, or deployed, and it stresses independent review to uncover risks before deployment. In the United States, social media ranking systems face no comparable general requirement to be evaluated at the design stage, so scrutiny has largely come after harm has occurred, often through litigation. Europe has started to move: the EU's Digital Services Act requires very large platforms to assess systemic risks from their algorithmic systems before deploying high-impact features, and the UK's Online Safety Act requires a new children's risk assessment before any significant change to a service's design or operation.

ledger.text: A design-first approach would require platforms to answer the same questions an auditor would ask: what requirement applies, what evidence proves it, who reviewed the evidence, what failed, and what changed because of the finding. An overall accuracy figure, verbal assurances, or informal promises to fix issues later count as weak evidence.

ledger.text: LIME's top reason held in {{sim.lime_top_reason_runs}} of {{sim.lime_reruns}} reruns and didn't change across kernel widths, and SHAP's top three features didn't change when the post was altered slightly. Stability still has to be tested rather than assumed, because LIME's sampling makes every run slightly different.
ledger.where: Site: Technical lens, Stability; Poster: five tests scorecard

ledger.text: Not tested with real users in this project. Judged against the intended audience, a SHAP value in {{sim.shap_units}} is not something a {{sim.persona_age}}-year-old or a legislator can act on, and the only actionable counterfactual puts the burden on the child rather than on the platform.
ledger.where: Site: Technical lens, Human usefulness; Poster: five tests scorecard

ledger.text: Announced in December 2022 for rollout over the following weeks, it gives short reasons such as that a video is similar to content the user has interacted with or searched for, is from an account the user follows, or is popular or was posted recently in the user's region.
ledger.where: Site: Public lens, TikTok

ledger.text: Popular Science reported that TikTok's "Why this video" feature would not reveal any major details about how the algorithm works and would give users only a hint as to why a video was shown. TikTok itself presented the feature as a step toward "meaningful transparency" and said it would expand it to bring "more granularity and transparency."
ledger.where: Site: Public lens, TikTok limits

ledger.text: In June 2023, Meta released 22 system cards describing how AI ranks content across Facebook and Instagram, and said it would expand "Why Am I Seeing This?" to Instagram's Reels tab and Explore and to Facebook Reels in the coming weeks, letting users tap an individual reel to see how their previous activity may have informed the models that shape the reels they see.
ledger.where: Site: Public lens, Meta

ledger.text: Meta states that there is a limit to what it can disclose safely, including the signals it uses to keep bad content out of Feeds, because disclosing them might make it easier to circumvent its defenses, and it acknowledges that not everyone will find information just because it is published on its website.
ledger.where: Site: Public lens, Meta limits

ledger.text: Under the EU Digital Services Act, very large platforms must offer at least one option for each of their recommender systems that is not based on profiling (Art. 38). Users must be able to switch to it at any time from the part of the interface where the feed is ranked (Art. 27(3); Recital 94).
ledger.where: Site: Public lens, EU non-profiling option

ledger.text: Researchers have cited a civil society complaint alleging that Meta is not meaningfully implementing these recommender requirements on Facebook and Instagram. In a separate case brought by Bits of Freedom, a Dutch court found in October 2025 that Meta was not complying with DSA Articles 27(3) and 38, and the Court of Appeal upheld that ruling in March 2026.
ledger.where: Site: Public lens, EU limits

ledger.text: Go back to the simulated teen. The reason a platform would most likely show her, paraphrasing TikTok's "Why this video," is "{{sim.platform_reason}}." It's accurate. It also accounts for only {{sim.platform_reason_share_pct}}% of why the top post ranked first. It doesn't tell her that {{sim.shap_top_feature}} was the largest single factor. And the only change it implies she can make, engaging less with similar content, wouldn't move the post off the top of her feed.
ledger.where: Site: Public lens, gap; Poster: Public quadrant

ledger.text: In March 2026, two juries reached verdicts against Meta within a day of each other: a Los Angeles jury found Meta and YouTube negligent in a case focused on design features such as infinite scroll and autoplay, and a New Mexico jury imposed a $375 million penalty in a case that included algorithms prioritizing sensational or harmful content.
ledger.where: Site: Public lens, stakes; Poster: Public quadrant

ledger.text: These dynamics are not limited to young users: Amnesty International found that Facebook's engagement-driven news feed, ranking and recommendation algorithms amplified anti-Rohingya hatred in Myanmar in the years before the 2017 atrocities (which the US government has determined to be genocide), and that Meta's later fixes, such as banning military leaders' accounts and adding Burmese-language moderators, focused on content moderation rather than on changing those algorithms.
